summary: Presents a checklist for evaluating MIME-capable user agents and describes access to a MIME test-responder that sends test messages. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 1844.

plainLanguage.summary: A to-do list to test whether an email program can handle pictures, sounds and other extras.

questions: how to test a mime mail client
how do you test email programs
subtitle: A to-do list for testing whether an email client can handle multimedia attachments.

tldr.problem: Email programs were starting to support multimedia content like images and audio, but there was no standard way to evaluate whether a client handled all the MIME features correctly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC provides a comprehensive checklist for testing MIME-capable user agents, covering basic functionality, protocol support, and handling of different content types and encodings.
tldr.outcome: It was replaced by RFC 1844 but served as a practical guide for vendors and system managers to test and improve their email clients' multimedia capabilities.

today: RFC 1820 was replaced by RFC 1844, so it is no longer the current standard for testing MIME user agents. However, the testing methodology it describes remains relevant as a practical framework for evaluating email client capabilities.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 1820 presents a checklist designed to evaluate whether email user agents properly support MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions). The checklist is not a strict conformance test but rather a practical guide from an implementation perspective, aimed at users and system managers deciding which email client to deploy.

The RFC encourages vendors, implementors and users to test their products against this checklist. Results can be submitted to a test responder service, and the RFC notes that vendors are encouraged to use the results to improve their products.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is a practical test sheet, not a strict rule book. It helps people figure out if an email program works well with pictures, sounds and other multimedia content.

sections.title: Test Messages and Submission
sections.content:
The RFC describes how to obtain test messages by sending email to a test responder service. By sending mail with a subject line containing a MIME content type (such as image/gif or audio/basic), the responder sends back a test message with that content type, allowing users to verify their client handles it correctly.

The RFC lists 21 different test message types available through this service, including text formats, images, audio, video, application files, multipart messages, and custom content types to test how clients handle undefined types.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives you an email address to write to. Tell it what kind of file you want to test (like a picture or sound), and it sends you a sample email. Then you see if your email program handles it properly.

sections.title: General Product Information
sections.content:
The checklist begins with sections covering product identification, installation, and configuration. Questions cover the product name and version, manufacturer information, supported platforms, installation complexity, system requirements, and licensing details (public domain, shareware, commercial or non-profit only).

System managers also need to know whether the client can be configured at the system level, whether it supports logging and accounting, and what size restrictions might apply to messages, message counts or folder limits. Security of the user's mailbox is another concern checked in this section.
sections.plainLanguage: First, we need to know about the program itself: what is it called, who made it, what computers does it run on, how hard is it to install, and how much does it cost?

sections.title: Protocol Support and Message Handling
sections.content:
The checklist examines which protocols the client supports for receiving and sending messages. It checks for SMTP (simple mail transfer), ESMTP (extended SMTP), POP (Post Office Protocol), IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol), or direct connection to a mail server (MTA). The client's user interface type (graphical or character-based) is also noted.

Basic email operations are verified: can users list, read, delete, and compose messages? Does it support reply, forward, and distribute operations? Which header fields (To, Cc, Bcc, From, Reply-To, Subject) does it generate correctly and allow users to set? Does it support filing mail into folders, filtering, sorting and address lists?
sections.plainLanguage: Next we check what the program actually does. Can you send and receive mail? Can you reply and forward messages? Can you organize mail into folders? Can you set up rules to sort incoming mail automatically?

sections.title: MIME Content Support
sections.content:
The largest section of the checklist focuses on MIME support. It verifies which content types the client can display or save: text, images (GIF, JPEG), audio, video, PostScript, and application files. For each type, the checklist asks whether the client displays it inline, requires printing, needs an external viewer, and whether a suitable viewer is pre-configured or included with the software.

The checklist covers multipart messages (mixed, parallel, digest, alternative) and asks how the client handles unknown or user-defined content types. It also checks which content-encodings are supported: 7-bit, quoted-printable, base64, 8-bit, and binary. Character set support (like ISO-8859-1) and support for non-ASCII characters in headers are tested as well.
sections.plainLanguage: The main test: can your email program handle pictures, sounds, videos and other stuff? For each type, we check if it can show it, print it, or needs another program to open it.

sections.title: Security and Testing Safety
sections.content: The RFC warns that testing a MIME user agent against this checklist involves the security risks described in the MIME specification (RFC 1521). Most notably, automatically executing PostScript interpreters presents serious security risks. Readers are encouraged to review the MIME specification for detailed security considerations before performing comprehensive tests.
sections.plainLanguage: Be careful when testing. Some of the stuff you test with (like PostScript files) can be dangerous if not handled safely. Read the safety instructions before you start testing.
